line: The kettle was in the middle of a sentence, and nobody had told it how the sentence ended.
The kettle had boiled for people for eleven years and had never once been asked what it thought.
The egg had been eyeing the bin all week.
The last egg had heard the others talk about the floor, and had decided to see for itself.
The dog had promised the stick it would fit, and the stick had believed him.
The dog kept a list in his head of everyone who had ever left, and in his opinion every one of them was coming back.
The cat sat on the exact spot where the sun was going to be, and the sun, being polite, came.
The cat had been guarding the doorway for no one in particular, which is the hardest kind of guarding.
The coffee gave up its heat a degree at a time, like a guest leaving a party who doesn't want to make a fuss.
The coffee went cold out of tact; it could see you were busy.
The tea went the colour of the afternoon and stayed there.
The teabag had opinions about being squeezed and kept them in the cup.
The toast popped up looking like something that had thought it over all night.
The toast landed butter-side up, because it knew who was watching.
The porridge pan had decided to forgive you, but only if you said sorry to the spoon first.
The porridge bubbled in a language only the wooden spoon spoke, and the spoon wasn't telling.
The loaf had been waiting all week to be the good news.
The bread kept its crust hard so that nobody would ask what it was like inside.
The soup simmered over a thought it hadn't decided to have yet.
For one spoonful the soup tasted like the kitchen it was remembering.
The milk knew the date on its side was only a suggestion, and was thinking hard about it.
The milk went round the cup once, like someone changing their mind.
The mug had a chip on its rim that it kept like a medal.
The cup held onto the warmth after you'd gone, in case you came back for it.
The pan had a burn on its bottom in the shape of a country nobody had named yet.
The pan hung on its hook and held a grudge against the whole cooker.
The fridge hummed one long note it had been holding since winter.
The fridge light came on for you and went out the moment you looked away, to find out what that was like.
The door had a way of staying nearly closed that made everyone in the house lower their voice.
The door knew everyone's footsteps and hadn't decided yet about yours.
The keys sat on the hook counting themselves, one short, as they did every night.
The key had been lost twice and now went to the same pocket every time, out of spite.
The window kept a small piece of every morning on its glass until somebody wiped it away.
The window liked the view and thought very little of the curtains.
The third stair had said one word in the night and refused to say it again.
The stairs went up one more step than they came down, and nobody had ever mentioned it.
The bus took the corner as if it had been asked a hard question.
The bus knew everyone's stop and was too polite to mention the ones they kept missing.
The train went through the dark with all its windows lit, like a long sentence nobody was reading aloud.
The train had been somewhere else all day and was slightly proud of it.
The car knew the way home so well that it was a little offended when you used the map.
The car warmed up slowly, and in that time it told the engine everything.
The bike leaned on the wall as if it had come from a much longer ride.
The bike's bell wanted very badly to be rung at a dog.
The rain was only checking that the glass still knew its name.
The rain had come a long way to tell the roof one small thing, and it said it over and over.
The wind went through the coats on the hooks and asked each one a question.
The wind tried every door on the street and found them all in the middle of something.
The snow covered the garden's mistakes first.
The snow stayed quiet on purpose, to hear what the street sounded like without anyone's help.
The sunlight took the long way across the kitchen, stopping at everything it liked.
The sun came in and lay on the floor as if it had a right to.
The moon kept its one good side to the house and hoped nobody asked about the other.
The moon looked in at the window the way it always did, to see if the house had changed its mind about anything.
The tree had stood there so long that it considered the street a rumour.
The tree held its leaves out like a hand that hadn't decided what to ask for.
The leaves came down in the order they had agreed on, and nobody fell early.
The leaves went along the pavement in a small rush, arguing about which way was home.
The garden was doing a great deal when nobody was looking, and stopped the moment you did.
The garden kept its own hours, and none of them were yours.
The pigeon, who had never once waved back, gave a very small bow.
The bird sat on the wire and told the street exactly what it thought, in one note.
The phone lay face-down on the table, listening to the room with the one ear it had.
The phone lit up for no one and went dark again, embarrassed.
The laptop fan sighed like someone being asked for one more thing.
The screen kept the shape of the last page you'd read, in case you wanted it back.
The clock was four minutes fast out of nerves, and would hear no argument.
The watch kept going on a wrist the way a very small animal keeps going.
The glasses stayed on and kept watch, so that the person under them could finally stop.
The glasses had seen everything you'd read this year and were keeping very quiet about it.
The shoes by the door stood in a nervous half-circle, waiting to be told where they were going.
The left shoe had gone one place further than the right all week, and the right was sore about it.
The coat held the shape of your shoulders for a while after you took it off, in case of questions.
The coat on the hook kept one pocket empty on purpose, for the day it was needed.
The umbrella opened with the look of something that had been proved right.
The umbrella had no idea it was the only thing between you and the whole sky, and it was better off.
The scarf had long ago given up on being a straight line.
The hat knew exactly what you looked like at your worst and had agreed to cover it.
The bed kept the dent of the night before, as if it were holding your place in a long queue.
The bed waited all day with its corner turned down, like an open door.
The pillow kept everything that was ever said into it and had never once repeated any of it.
The pillow had two sides and kept the cool one for later.
The sofa took the whole of your weight and said nothing, which is what it was for.
The empty chair kept its arms slightly open in case anyone changed their mind.
The table bore the ring of every cup it had ever forgiven.
The table stood on three legs and one decision.
The lamp made a small round room inside the larger room and stayed in it.
The light in the hall came on one second late, as though it had to be told twice.
The candle burned down by hours and did not once complain about the hours.
The flame leaned toward whoever was talking.
The book lay open at the page it had been told to keep.
The book had a spine that remembered every place it had been bent.
The pen had one sentence left in it and was saving it.
The notebook lay shut on the table, being very careful not to know anything yet.
The letter lay face-down on the mat, thinking about being read.
The envelope was sealed so tightly that it was holding its breath.
The mirror was always the last to know.
The mirror kept its best angle for whoever wasn't looking.
The bath filled slowly, listening to itself fill.
The shower sang one note until the water was hot, and then fell silent out of respect.
The washing went round and round in the machine, telling itself it was a tide.
The shirts hung on the line with their arms out, practising.
The dishes stacked up in the sink and held a small, damp parliament.
The plates leaned on each other in the rack the way people do at the end of a long evening.
The bin took everything in and kept a poker face about all of it.
The bin was as full as it could be and had one more thing in it than that.
The hoover went round the room roaring at what it found, and was always disappointed in the dust.
The broom stood in its corner with the posture of something that had once been told it could fly.
The plant on the sill leaned toward the window as though the window had said something.
The flowers in the jar had stopped being cut flowers and were just flowers now, and held their heads like it.
The song ended, and the room kept the shape of it a moment longer.
The radio talked low to itself in the kitchen, in a voice that knew all the old songs.
The supermarket hummed its one bright note over every aisle, and nobody in it looked up.
The shop bell rang for you as though it had been saving it.
The bag held more than it showed and less than it promised.
The bag sat by the door, already thinking about the journey.
The ticket in the pocket was soft at the corners from waiting.
The ticket had a time on it and meant it.
The sandwich was cut in half, and each half missed the other.
The sandwich held together out of loyalty.
The cake sat under its cloth and knew exactly how it would be remembered.
The biscuit tin rattled once, to say it was still a tin of biscuits and not a tin of anything else.
The apple was red on one side as a matter of principle.
The fruit bowl sat in the middle of the table, pretending not to be waiting for anyone.
The dinner went on the table in the order of its feelings.
The pot on the cooker kept the last of the dinner warm for a second helping that might still come.
The river had somewhere to be and said so quietly all day.
The river carried the sky along without ever once dropping it.
The road went on ahead of you with the air of knowing the way.
The pavement kept the day's footsteps in its cracks and gave none of them away.
The sea took everything in and kept the shape of none of it.
The waves came up the beach to ask the same question and went back for the answer.
The gate leaned on its post like someone who'd been told the news.
The wall had held up its end of things for a hundred years and wanted it noted.
The bench had been waiting for the right person to sit down and had decided that anyone would do.
The park kept its quiet in the middle, where the grass was longest.
The cloud over the roofs had lost its way and was too proud to ask.
The sky was the colour of the inside of a shell and did not mean anything by it.
The stick had never wanted to go through the gate and was not about to start.
The stick lay in the grass, certain it was a sword.
The spoon in the drawer had stirred more secrets than any priest.
The knives lay in their tray like a row of people who had agreed not to talk.
The rug had been walked across so often it had stopped minding and started listening.
The floor kept every footstep it had ever been given.
The oven ticked as it cooled, counting the whole evening back to nothing.
The cooker had a ring that came on slowly, like a thought.
The machine ended its song with a small, satisfied click, like a person finishing a hard sum.
The dryer kept the warmth of a day that had gone somewhere else.
The lunch was eaten in the time it takes a clock to forgive you.
The sandwich held together out of loyalty, which is more than can be said for the afternoon.
The breakfast table was set for a better day than the one that came.
The breakfast things sat out until noon, like guests who hadn't been told it was over.
The fog had come in to look for something and was too polite to say what.
The fog sat on the road and let the cars be sorry first.
The thunder rolled around the sky like furniture being moved in the flat upstairs.
The storm made a great deal of noise about a very small decision.
The frost wrote on the windscreen in a hand nobody could read, and was proud of it.
The ice on the puddle kept the shape of the sky it had been given.
The morning came in on tiptoe and turned the radio on by accident.
The morning had been folded very small and put in the day's top pocket.
The night went round the house turning things over, checking they were all still there.
The night arrived in the order the lamps asked for it.
October had been left on all the pavements, and was beginning to be trodden in.
The autumn smelled of the inside of a coat that had been somewhere good.
The onions made their case and everyone in the kitchen wept with them.
The garlic went into the pan with the confidence of something that had never been to a funeral.
The pasta turned in the pot slowly, as if reading the water.
The rice swelled until it had opinions.
The pizza box sat on the table with its lid up, like a mouth that has just said something.
The chips went cold at exactly the speed of a good conversation.
The chocolate broke into its squares along the lines it had been practising.
The sweet sat in the bowl, certain it was the one.
The wine sat in the glass thinking about being grapes.
The pint went down by the ordinary amount and was flat by the end of the story.
The butter softened slowly, like someone being told a kind thing.
The jam had been waiting at the back of the cupboard for exactly this slice of toast.
The potatoes sat in their sack and gossiped about the weather underground.
The carrots had decided to be orange about it.
The jar would not open for anyone, and was not sorry.
The bottle held on to the last inch of itself with great dignity.
The parcel on the step had come a very long way to be left with nobody in.
The box held the shape of what had been in it for a week after.
The boiler cleared its throat before every thought.
The radiator ticked as it warmed, like a small animal deciding to trust the room.
The kitchen kept its own hours and a drawer for everything it had forgiven.
The kitchen smelled of three different days at once and was fond of all of them.
The hall light came on for the shoes and nobody else.
The hallway listened to everything that was said in it and kept the good bits.
The bathroom tap held one drop back, for later.
The towel on the rail had been warm once and remembered it.
The drawer held three batteries, a key and a promise, and none of them worked.
The cupboard door swung open a hand's width, as if the cupboard had just thought of something.
The curtains held the dark back with one hand.
The curtain moved once, though there was no draught to blame it on.
The gutter carried the rain away like a rumour it didn't believe.
The chimney stood in the sky with its hands in its pockets.
The smell went through the flat first and told the rooms what to expect.
The smell had already been in every room by the time you noticed it.
The noise from the next room stopped as soon as it was listened for.
The creak in the floor said the same word it always said, a little louder for company.
The dust settled on the shelf the way a cat settles, after much deliberation.
The dust kept a careful record of everything that had not been moved.
The spider had put a great deal of thought into the corner and wanted it noted.
The web caught the morning and held it up to the light for approval.
The moth went round the lamp like someone trying to remember a name.
The bee crossed the kitchen as though it had an appointment.
The fox crossed the road as if the road had been laid for him.
The squirrel ran along the fence with its news and could not be stopped.
The ducks went by in a line, each one convinced the others were following.
The swan held the whole pond up on its back and looked cross about it.
The sheep looked up at the same moment, as if they had been told something.
The horse stood in the field holding very still, to see if the field would move first.
The heron stood in the shallows like it had been asked to wait and was determined to do it properly.
The heron kept one leg in reserve.
The snail crossed the path with the whole of its house and none of its doubts.
The worm came up after the rain to see what all the noise had been.
The lift thought about the ground floor for a long time before agreeing to it.
The escalator took everyone up at exactly the speed of their own mistakes.
The taxi waited at the kerb with its light on, like a very patient idea.
The cab knew the city by its corners and its grudges.
The plane drew a white line across the sky and then thought better of it.
The boat knocked at the harbour wall all night like a dog that wanted letting in.
The platform waited for the train the way a dog waits for a name.
The timetable on the wall had a plan and was not about to share it.
The traffic lights changed their minds three times in your favour and once against.
The roundabout kept everyone going round in case they remembered what they'd come for.
The church bell struck the hour and then a second time, very quietly, for the one it had missed.
The steeple held a piece of the sky in place.
The pub had kept its warmth through the afternoon for exactly this.
The cafe window had steamed up to give everyone inside a little privacy.
The playground was quiet in the way a bell is quiet before it goes.
The classroom clock had been watching the same afternoon since September.
The library hummed with all the sentences it was not allowed to say aloud.
The library kept every book's secret in alphabetical order.
The printer thought about each page as though it were signing it.
The meeting room had a table too big for what was said around it.
The queue moved forward one person at a time, like a thought being slowly agreed upon.
The post office smelled of string, paper and other people's good news.
The corridor went on a little longer than the plan said, out of tact.
The signal came and went like a small shy animal at the edge of the room.
The charger lay on the floor with its one hand out.
The headphones kept the whole street out and one song in.
The podcast went on talking in the kitchen to nobody, and was happy.
The photograph kept the afternoon exactly as it had been and was a little tired of it.
The picture on the wall had been looking at the same view for years and had opinions.
The list on the fridge had one item crossed out so hard that it showed through.
The receipt in the pocket remembered the whole afternoon and could not stop itself.
The map had never once agreed with the road.
The map was folded wrong along a line that had been right for years.
The coin had been to a great many hands and brought back nothing but the weather.
The wallet held the whole week flat and folded.
The button hung by one thread and was very calm about it.
The needle went in and out of the cloth like a very small, well-meaning argument.
The ladder leaned against the wall as if it had been told a secret and was holding it up for you to see.
The hammer lay where it was left and dreamed of being exactly the right size.
The torch made a small yellow room in the dark and invited the moths in.
The match flared once, to show it could.
The string had been tied in a knot nobody could remember agreeing to.
The tape peeled up at the corner like a small, sticky question.
The balloon lowered itself a little each day, out of manners.
The puzzle was missing one piece and had stopped mentioning it.
The piano in the corner held every song it had been taught and played none of them unasked.
The guitar leaned in its case with the look of something that had just been told a joke.
The odd sock had been looking for its other half so long it had forgotten what it looked like.
The pyjamas were warm from the airing cupboard and ready to be told everything.
The slippers waited by the bed with their mouths open, ready for the day's news.
The wellies stood in the porch with the mud of a whole field in them.
The toothbrush stood to attention in the mug and awaited the day's orders.
The soap had been used so long that it was mostly an idea.
The sleep came in sideways, like a cat through a half-open door.
The dream waited behind the eyelids until the room was properly dark.
The tiredness sat down in the chair behind you and asked nothing.
The laugh got out before the rest of the sentence and had to be waited for.
The joke sat in the room afterwards, pleased with itself and a little embarrassed.
The oven glove held on to the heat of everything it had ever touched.
The tea towel had dried the world and was still damp about it.
The pebble in the pocket had been a mountain once and did not mention it.
The shell kept the sea in the back of its mind and hummed it when asked.
The tulips leaned out of the vase to see who was talking.
The sunflower turned its face to the window and then to you, on principle.
The path ran on ahead and waited at every bend, pretending to look at something else.
The hill took the whole sky on its shoulders and went on being a hill.
The bridge held the river up to the light and let it carry on.
The tunnel kept a little of last night in the middle, to be sure.
The fire talked to itself in the grate, softly, in a language of small collapses.
The embers kept the shape of the log for as long as they could.
The puddle had the sky in it and was a little proud of the arrangement.
The tap dripped on at its own count, patient as a priest.
The shadow lay along the floor and waited for the lamp to change its mind.
The shadow of the chair stretched out and tried the door.
The quiet filled up the room like water finding its level.
The silence was the kind that has been left on purpose.
The dog had promised the stick it would fit, and the stick had believed him.
The dog walked into the wind with his ears doing all the talking.
The dog ran the whole park twice, to make sure it was still all there.
The cat lay across the keyboard and typed the only sentence she'd ever meant.
The cat watched the street from the sill with the interest of a landlord.
The egg had been eyeing the bin all week.
The egg sat in its cup like a small bald king waiting for the knock.
The bus pulled away from the stop with the look of someone leaving a party at exactly the wrong moment.
The train carried the window along and let the fields come and go in it like thoughts.
The rain found the one gap in the coat and was thorough about it.
The coffee went cold out of tact; it could see you were busy.
The coffee steamed up in the cup like a tiny, hopeful weather system.
The tea ran across the table to see how far it could get, and got as far as the letter.
The sofa took the whole of her weight and said nothing, which is what it was for.
The glasses stayed on and kept watch, so that the person under them could finally stop.
The phone went dark in the middle of its own sentence, and the room got larger.
The phone rang the way it always did, as if it were bringing news of a death or an offer.
The key had been lost twice and now went to the same pocket every time, out of spite.
The key was cut for a lock that had been taken down years ago, and still hoped.
The flame leaned toward whoever was talking.
The book lay open at the page it had been told to keep.
The bread had gone hard to protect what was left of it.
The dough rose slowly, like a rumour in a small town.
The river walked along beside you and kept up its end of the conversation.
The road home was longer than the road out, by the exact length of the day.
The mirror held the crack like a secret it had agreed not to repeat.
The mirror carried the street along with it and was careful not to spill any.
The tree had gone orange all at once, because it had been told, and it was keeping very quiet about who told it.
The leaves rose when kicked and settled again in a slightly better arrangement.
The snow was in the forecast and the forecast was feeling smug.
The moon came down the stairs of the garden one white step at a time.
The sunlight lay on the floor at three o'clock like a rug that someone had paid a great deal for.
The fridge hummed the same low note the whole house had been tuned to.
The washing machine finished mid-sentence of the day and waited to be forgiven.
The heron stood in the shallows like it had been asked to wait and was determined to do it properly.
The pigeon walked in as if the shop had been built round it, looked at everything, and walked out.
The pigeon, who had never once waved back, gave a very small bow.
The cake was exactly as big as the occasion and not one crumb bigger.
The plant leaned away from you with great tact, toward the thing it actually wanted.
The smell of onions went through the flat and told every room it was staying for supper.
The letter lay on the table, damp at one corner, thinking again about what it had been going to say.
The shop bell rang for you as though it had been saving it.
The corridor went on a little longer than the plan said, out of tact.
The ceiling tiles held still to be counted, and kept their own total.
The boiler ticked in the dark like a very small clock that has lost its owner.
